title: Multiple Routes to Affiliation: Children Give Greater Weight to Shared Preferences Affording Broader Relational Benefits
abstract: ABSTRACT While it is well‐established that similarity drives affiliation, not all similarities afford the same relational benefits. Using a third‐party friendship inference task, we found that elementary‐age children in Japan ( N = 65; age 6 to 11; 32 female) were sensitive to how widely shared preferences are when making affiliative judgements. Specifically, children were shown a character with two preferences, each shared with a different potential friend. The more widely shared children perceived one preference to be relative to the other, the more likely they were to expect the character to befriend the person who shared that preference ( B = 0.23, SE = 0.04, p < 0.001, OR = 1.26). Because widely shared similarities can connect individuals to larger social circles offering greater acceptance, networks, and resources, children may view these affiliative pathways as more strategic than those based on narrowly shared similarities, which may signal deeper compatibility but offer fewer relational benefits overall.
